kagan.tagline: Careful interpretation gives democratic government room to work and constitutional rights room to develop, with existing law setting the terms.
kagan.bio: Kagan reads law as the product of institutions making decisions together over time. Understanding a statute means understanding the practical arrangement its words establish, including choices Congress left for others to make. Constitutional guarantees also acquire substance through generations of judicial decisions; their earliest applications don’t exhaust their reach. Judges can draw out further implications, but must justify them through that accumulated legal work. This explains her combination of contextual textualism and an evolving Constitution: legal judgment has a constructive role, while the authority to exercise it comes with obligations to decisions beyond the judge’s own.

hugo_black.tagline: Written constitutional guarantees protect liberty by binding judges as firmly as lawmakers to the rights the people have already secured.
hugo_black.bio: Black believed putting rights into a written Constitution settled choices that officials should no longer be free to reconsider. Judges must determine those guarantees’ meaning through text and history, then enforce them even when they consider the results unwise. That conviction drove both his resistance to balancing away freedom of speech and his insistence that the Bill of Rights bind state governments. It also explains his rejection of judges creating broader rights from their own ideas of fairness. Outside the Constitution’s restrictions, elected lawmakers could make choices he disliked. His distrust of judicial discretion was itself a theory of how to keep liberty secure.
